reference.source: Resnick Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
clinicalPearls: Osteopathia striata is a sclerosing bone dysplasia defined radiologically by fine linear longitudinal striations in the metaphyses and diaphyses of long bones and a fan-like pattern in the iliac wings.
Isolated osteopathia striata (Voorhoeve disease) is usually an asymptomatic incidental radiographic finding of no clinical consequence.

When combined with cranial sclerosis it forms an X-linked disorder caused by AMER1 (WTX) mutations, typically more severe in affected males and often lethal or with major anomalies in hemizygous males.
Females with osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis characteristically have macrocephaly, cranial nerve compression with hearing loss, and cleft palate.
The striations run parallel to the long axis of the bone and do not disturb bone modelling or cause pathological fracture in the isolated form.
It is one of the classic mixed sclerosing bone dysplasias and may coexist with osteopoikilosis and melorheostosis.
Bone scintigraphy is typically normal, helping distinguish it from active sclerotic processes such as metastasis or osteomyelitis.
Recognition matters chiefly to avoid unnecessary investigation of an incidental benign pattern.
reference.pathophysiology: The isolated form is a sporadic or benign developmental anomaly of endochondral ossification in which longitudinal columns of persistent dense trabecular bone produce the characteristic striations without disturbing overall bone architecture. The syndromic osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis results from loss-of-function mutations in AMER1, which encodes a negative regulator of the canonical Wnt/beta-catenin signalling pathway central to osteoblast activity. Loss of this brake enhances Wnt signalling and osteoblastic bone formation, producing the striations in long bones together with sclerotic overgrowth of the skull base and vault. The X-linked pattern and X-inactivation account for the milder mosaic phenotype in females and the severe or lethal presentation in hemizygous males.
additionalInvestigations: plain radiography of long bones and pelvis for striation pattern
skull radiography or CT for cranial sclerosis in syndromic cases
bone scintigraphy to demonstrate absent increased uptake
audiometry when cranial nerve involvement is suspected
AMER1 gene sequencing in syndromic presentations
serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase to exclude metabolic bone disease
redFlags: progressive hearing loss or other cranial neuropathy suggesting foraminal narrowing
macrocephaly with developmental concern in an infant
severe skeletal or visceral anomalies in a male fetus or neonate
unexpected sclerotic lesions with abnormal tracer uptake prompting reappraisal
reference.prognosis: Isolated osteopathia striata is benign with a normal life expectancy and requires no treatment; the syndromic form carries morbidity from cranial nerve compression and craniofacial anomalies and may be lethal in affected males.
pitfalls: Mistaking incidental striations for sclerotic metastases and initiating an oncological work-up.
Overlooking associated cranial sclerosis and its neurological consequences by imaging long bones alone.
Failing to offer genetic counselling once the X-linked syndromic form is recognised.
Confusing the linear striations with the rounded foci of osteopoikilosis.
Attributing hearing loss to unrelated causes rather than foraminal stenosis.
references: Resnick Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders, current edition
Taybi and Lachman Radiology of Syndromes, Metabolic Disorders and Skeletal Dysplasias
management: Reassure and avoid intervention in isolated (Voorhoeve) disease, which is a benign incidental radiographic finding of no clinical consequence
Confirm the diagnosis on plain radiography and use bone scintigraphy showing absent uptake to distinguish the striations from osteoblastic metastases
Check serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase to exclude a metabolic bone disorder
Distinguish the isolated form from osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis, arranging AMER1 sequencing where cranial or craniofacial features are present
Arrange audiometry and cranial-nerve assessment when the syndromic form with skull-base sclerosis is suspected
Offer clinical genetics referral and family assessment for the X-linked syndromic form
